 Santa Rosa declares local emergency ahead of strengthening El Niño 
 The declaration is a proactive step the city is taking to prepare for any inclement weather this winter.

 By Dylan Sherman | dylan.sherman@pressdemocrat.com PUBLISHED: November 15, 2026 at 9:00 AM PST | UPDATED: November 18, 2026 at 10:05 AM PST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Santa Rosa has become the third local government to adopt an emergency proclamation as the region heads into the wet season and braces for potentially greater flood risk posed by a strengthening El Niño system. 
 The declaration, which the City Council approved Tuesday, Nov. 10, formally recognizes the threat of severe weather on city infrastructure and authorizes the city manager to coordinate appropriate response.
 “The message we want to convey is that the city is ready,” Fire Chief Scott Westrope told council members.
 The proactive step provides city officials additional flexibility to mobilize resources, streamline emergency-related purchases and to pursue state or federal assistance if needed.

 El Niño is not a storm but a weather pattern that results in a warming of the tropical eastern Pacific Ocean, which can have large-scale climate effects around the world. Some consequences include increased rainfall and destructive flooding, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
 Meteorologists expect the developing El Niño to strengthen into a “Super El Niño” as ocean temperatures continue to rise, bringing even more severe weather that could exacerbate flooding and coastal erosion.
 Though the impact in more inland areas such as Santa Rosa is unclear, intense weather could cause localized flooding, overburden the city’s creeks and stormwater systems, and cause potential landslides in hillside areas. Fallen trees as well as damage to public infrastructure and private property from other storm-related debris, electrical outages and transportation disruptions, are other concerns.
 “There is a high likelihood, an 83% chance, of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950,” Westrope said. “The message is El Niño is here. El Niño will be here through the winter.”
 The proclamation, approved 6-0, follows similar emergency declarations adopted by Cloverdale and Sonoma County and came ahead of dangerous surf predicted along the Sonoma County coastline as well as the region’s first substantial rain during a pair of storms that began on Friday. Vice Mayor Jeff Okrepkie was absent.
 It’s one component of the city’s broader preparedness efforts underway across multiple departments. The city also is conducting specialized training for staff, preparing equipment, addressing critical infrastructure maintenance and coordinating resources ahead of the rainy season.
 The Transportation and Public Works Department has targeted strategic drainage repairs, maintenance of city-operated drainage facilities and creeks.

 Outside of maintenance work, the city is also monitoring weather forecasts and creek conditions and preparing public information and sandbag resources as warranted. The city’s sandbag station, located at 55 Stony Point Rd., will only be open during significant rain events.
 The resolution requires the City Council review it at least every 60 days and it can be terminated early if conditions warrant it.
 Westrope said residents also should prepare ahead of time, similar to how the community prepares for wildfire threats, which can limit impacts to structures, businesses and residents’ wellbeing.
 Resident preparations include: clearing gutters and drains before heavy rains; checking emergency supplies and medications; creating a household emergency and evacuation plan; signing up for emergency alerts; checking weather conditions before traveling; avoid driving through flooded roadways and follow road closure and detour signs; and checking in on neighbors during severe weather.
 You can reach Staff Writer Dylan Sherman at dylan.sherman@pressdemocrat.com.
